results.finding: sections, unit counts and unit forms match the spec
Every aligned unit's outline summary states the controlling idea of its spec paragraph; the three callouts match no paragraph, as expected.
Only Reading ¶2 (p30) was marked two_ideas. It is a bridge: the questions apply to one's own systems, which the remaining sections take up. That is one transition, and the spec asks for exactly it.
Every unit advances the supporting claim its section declares; introduction, bridge and conclusion units trace to the thesis as a whole.
Each evidence item, table and quotation in the aligned text has a sentence saying what it shows. Figure captions were judged only through the readers' quotations of them (Figures 1, 4, 6, 9).

All boundaries express their declared relationship. One label is loose but not failed: p28's transition_in is declared 'example', while the paragraph opens with a question and the test and gives Kestrel & Pine last; the carry-over (boxes filled per stage) is picked up.

results.draft_locus: Setting the Scene at Kestrel & Pine: A Whiteboard in February 2027 ¶3
results.quote: "Two boxes were empty." followed by "Two more boxes were empty." I stopped to ask why four empty boxes were split into two bullets with nearly the same opening. (flow reader A, item 1; item 2 on the delivery promise: "left me unsure whether it has an owner or not")
results.finding: The lead promises 'Three things', but the list gives two bullets of the same kind, a sum ('that made four empty boxes') and a fifth item (the delivery promise, 'unowned in a smaller way'); both readers re-read to find what the three things were.

results.draft_locus: The Map: Six Layers ¶2
results.quote: "A layer is a group of capabilities that share a purpose and a rhythm (how fast their facts change), and the map has six." The definition made me expect each layer's rhythm in the sentences that follow. Each layer is then described by its purpose only ... I looked back to see whether I had missed it. (flow reader B, item 3)
results.finding: Both readers stumbled in the layers paragraph, anchored on the same sentence but for different reasons: B because 'rhythm' is promised and never given per layer, A because six layers and three abbreviations come in one run and the long EDI parenthesis broke the partners sentence. The 'purpose and a rhythm' wording is the spec's (p13); the density is the draft's.

results.draft_locus: The Map: Six Layers ¶3
results.quote: Product identity appears in three rows ... The customer likewise appears under both the ERP ("customer masters") and Identity and master data ... I could not tell which box is the home of "which product is this" or of the customer. For a table presented as "the chapter's main deliverable" this was the one place I could not use it as instructed. (flow reader B, item 4; item 5 on store stock counts)
results.finding: The capability table gives product identity three rows and the customer two against the one-home rule, and the three notes under it do not explain this.

results.draft_locus: How the Pieces Talk: The Typical Flows ¶2
results.quote: "Everything else tolerates some lag if there is a reconciliation behind it." The table just above asks for stock and availability in "Seconds to minutes at peak" ... I paused over how a flow needed within seconds "tolerates some lag". (flow reader A, item 9)
results.finding: The sentence is about exactness, the table cell about speed; the paragraph does not say so, and the reader needed a second reading.

results.draft_locus: Three Ways to Cover the Map ¶2
results.quote: "Adobe's October 2026 information center lists, next to three deployment options for Adobe Commerce (...), a separate product, Commerce Optimizer, that 'can work alongside ...'" I had to re-read to find the object of "lists". (flow reader A, item 10)
results.finding: The Adobe sentence separates the verb from its object with a long parenthesis; both readers read it twice. B adds that it makes the opposite point before the suite's definition is finished.

results.draft_locus: Three Ways to Cover the Map ¶3
results.quote: I lost what the paragraph was establishing. Lightspeed in particular is out of place: the paragraph is about hosted shop platforms and the evidence offered is a point-of-sale vendor's revenue split. (flow reader B, item 9)
results.finding: A POS vendor's revenue split is the evidence in a paragraph about hosted shop platforms; A thought the subject had changed, B lost the paragraph's point between prices, card rates, Lightspeed and the logistics sale. The spec assigns Lightspeed and four evidence items to this paragraph.

results.draft_locus: Three Ways to Cover the Map ¶5
results.quote: "Six of those eight ... are operational and partner boxes on the map, so one group supplies six boxes". The six include the POS. The map's own table puts Point of sale in the Experience layer ... the sentence does not agree with it. (flow reader B, item 11)
results.finding: Both readers stopped at the same sentence: B because the six include the POS, which the capability table puts in the experience layer; A because the count had to be rebuilt from the list and 'the storefront platform still bought elsewhere' follows an 'ERP-and-webshop product'. The claim is the spec's own evidence statement for p25.

results.draft_locus: Three Ways to Cover the Map ¶6
results.quote: The section promised three ways, then "two variants", and the table has four columns: one variant gets a column and the other does not ... there is no reason given for why the specialist group, also called a variant, gets one. (flow reader A, item 13)
results.finding: Three ways, two variants, four columns: both readers stopped to recount what the table compares; the draft explains why ERP-centered commerce has no column but not why the other variant has one. The grouping is the spec's (p25, p26). Reader A (item 14) also found 'group' meaning both stage 4 and the vendor group in the table.

results.draft_locus: Three Ways to Cover the Map ¶7
results.quote: I stumbled on "a merchant that is not a vendor". Nothing before it has discussed merchants who are vendors, so I did not know who is being excluded. (flow reader A, item 15)
results.finding: The qualifier excludes a group the chapter never introduces; the phrase is the spec's own (p26a, AC-5).

results.draft_locus: Reading a Vendor's Product Page Against the Map ¶1
results.quote: "your ERP stays the system of record" ... the quotation does not say which fact the ERP stays the record of. The example therefore did not show me the answer it was introduced to show. (flow reader B, item 13)
results.finding: The Fluent quotation is offered as a vendor stating which fact it owns, but names no fact, and reads against the later failure of an ERP used as the order hub.

results.draft_locus: Across Scale Stages: When It Fits and When It Limits ¶2
results.quote: "an OMS is overkill with one channel and one warehouse and overdue the day a second order source appears." This does not agree with the table directly above it ... I could not tell whether a stage 2 merchant should have an OMS. (flow reader B, item 14)
results.finding: Two one-reader points in this paragraph: B finds the OMS example against the stage table and the test; A (item 16) cannot tell 'producer' from 'writer', so more than one writer is an alarm in one section and a reason to buy in another. Both wordings are in the spec (p28).

results.draft_locus: When It Goes Wrong ¶1
results.quote: "Filling the right number of boxes is not enough ..." The fourth way, "The map copied from a giant", is exactly a case of filling the wrong number of boxes ... So the opening sentence promises four failures that lie beyond the scale question and one of the four is the scale question again. (flow reader B, item 15)
results.finding: The section's opening contrast does not hold for the fourth failure; the contrast is the spec's transition_in for the section.

results.draft_locus: When It Goes Wrong ¶2
results.quote: "(an illustrative figure, like the 600 variants)" The closing aside stopped me. The whole company is fictional, so I did not understand why these two figures are singled out as illustrative and the others (1,340 units, €96,000, €19,400) are not. (flow reader B, item 16)
results.finding: Both readers were stopped by the 'illustrative figure' aside. A adds a time problem: the outcome of naming the WMS as single writer (May 2027) is told before the decision (W1) is introduced, which comes from the spec's order.

results.draft_locus: When It Goes Wrong ¶3
results.quote: I re-read "because none was". I think it means "because no box was named for it either", but it first read as an unfinished sentence. (flow reader A, item 18)
results.finding: The elliptical clause 'because none was' reads as unfinished.

results.draft_locus: When It Goes Wrong ¶4
results.quote: "A box held by a vendor who sells a different box." The heading speaks of a vendor, but the examples and the detection are about a system in the merchant's own landscape (flow reader A, item 19)
results.finding: The bold label says 'vendor' where the body, Figure 9 and the spec (p36: 'a system that was bought for a different box') say system.

results.draft_locus: In Practice: Kestrel & Pine's Systems on the Map ¶1
results.quote: The scene says the box with six writers holds warehouse stock ... But the In Practice section says the warehouse is "simply covered ... by the WMS" and puts "six writers of stock" in the "Inventory and availability" row. I went back to the capability table to work out which box the six writers belong to and could not settle it. (flow reader A, item 4)
results.finding: One-reader points on the Kestrel & Pine table: A cannot place the six writers (warehouse box or availability row), cannot rebuild six from the four systems listed (item 5) and reads 'five jobs in one box' against the failure section (item 20); B meets a pricing overlap and 'System in January 2027' as new in a February whiteboard (items 18, 19). No cell was reported by both.

results.draft_locus: In Practice: Kestrel & Pine's Systems on the Map ¶2
results.quote: The decisions come in the order W3, W2, W1, W5, with W4 given three sections earlier. I checked that I had not missed one. The Trade-offs section also said the platform would be surrounded "with an OMS, a PIM and an availability service", which read as three products; here the availability service is a module of the OMS. (flow reader A, item 22)
results.finding: Decision numbers out of order, and the availability service is a third product in one section and a module of the OMS here.

results.draft_locus: Introduction callout
results.quote: The box promises three patterns. The Giant's Boots is named and treated in "When It Goes Wrong". The Spaghetti Junction is never named again ... I could not match the three promised patterns to the four failures of the body. (flow reader B, item 17)
results.finding: The opening callout names three failure patterns and the body four failures of its own; only one is picked up by name. The callout is house format outside the spec's paragraphs.

results.draft_locus: What to Take Away ¶2
results.quote: "the specialist boxes (OMS, PIM, WMS, returns, search, channel integration, iPaaS, payments) are distinct product categories with their own vendors and definitions, as the vendors' own November 2026 pages show." ... the chapter quoted definitions for two of these (an OMS and a PIM). I looked for the others and did not find them. (flow reader B, item 20)
results.finding: The take-away claims vendor definitions for eight categories; the body quotes two.

results.draft_locus: What to Take Away ¶3
results.quote: "A team of fourteen, the size of Kestrel & Pine's technology team, should expect to own joins, not boxes." The team size is new at this point in the chapter, and it appears in the takeaways, which otherwise only restate. "App governance" in the same bullet is also new. (flow reader A, item 23)
results.finding: The team of fourteen and 'app governance' appear for the first time in the take-aways; both readers went back to check whether they had missed them. Neither is in the spec's idea for p39.

results.draft_locus: Introduction callout
results.quote: "a platform plus apps covers the center and rents the edges" ... This is the hosted product, named "a platform" in a chapter whose title uses "Commerce Platform" for the whole set ... In the Key Points, before any gloss, it is close to blocking
results.finding: 'Platform' for the hosted shop platform is used in the Key Points long before 'hosted SaaS shop platform' is glossed, and the short form recurs in tables and captions, also for the vendor ('the platform is also a payments company').

results.draft_locus: Introduction callout
results.quote: "A suite covers many boxes with one vendor's data model". Never explained ... It is the core of the suite's definition ("in one data model").
results.finding: 'Data model' carries the definition of a suite and is never explained; the only help is 'decides what order and product mean'.

results.draft_locus: Three Ways to Cover the Map ¶6
results.quote: First use, trade-offs table: "Omnichannel and Group merchants with a platform team". It is never explained, and it is unclear which platform the team runs.
results.finding: 'Platform team' is used three times, the last as what best-of-breed needs, and never explained.

results.draft_locus: Three Ways to Cover the Map ¶4
results.quote: "MACH stands for microservices, API-first, cloud-native and headless; headless means the storefront is a separate application...". Only "headless" is explained. Its gloss introduces commerce engine, also unexplained.
results.finding: MACH is on the spec's does-not-know list; the draft expands it into four words and explains one. 'Microservices', 'API-first' and 'cloud-native' are left as they are.

results.draft_locus: Three Ways to Cover the Map ¶2
results.quote: "one platform across B2C, B2B, point of sale and order management". Never explained. The reader knows D2C and B2B, not B2C.
results.finding: The acronym B2C is not expanded; the criterion asks for every acronym to be expanded on first use.

results.draft_locus: Reading a Vendor's Product Page Against the Map ¶1
results.quote: "differ by a factor of six because users are seats". Never explained, and it is the whole point of the example.
results.finding: 'Seats' is the explanation offered for the customers-against-users example and is itself unexplained.
Opens on a concrete request (store pickup), bridges to the three questions and gives a full roadmap.
Judged as a whole: a synthesis paragraph, three labelled tiers, questions and a hand-off. The tiers recall body evidence by name without re-arguing it.

What to Take Away ¶1 states what no section states (one home, every other holder a copy fed by a flow, a product leaves the flows to the merchant) and why it matters (failures show on the map before the business).
What to Take Away ¶1 returns to the store-pickup request and places it on the map: three boxes and the flows between them, an app claiming one at most.
The intro reader predicted all nine sections in order, the kind of evidence (running example, vendors' public pages, tables) and the tone.

The reader names order management (holding and steering to fulfillment, which is the sourcing half) and says warehouse and fulfillment and inventory and availability are not included. The map has no separate 'sourcing' box, so the reader folds it into order management.
Every system looks complete from the inside; draw the jobs first, then place systems: overlap is one box with several names, gap an empty box.
Derived fact, available-to-promise, formula given, hand edit bypasses the calculation and lets the storefront promise what the warehouse cannot deliver.
Prices, orders and payments; the rest tolerate lag with a reconciliation behind them; finance as a daily batch.
States the rule in full and that the joins stay with the merchant whichever vendor it picks.
